sources.title: Back to school: 10 tips from a Developmental Paediatrician
sources.publisher: Queensland Health (Queensland Government), tips from developmental paediatrician Dr Angela Owens; published and last updated 30 January 2026
sources.quote: New routines, expectations, teachers and social dynamics can all be exhausting, so it’s very common for behaviour to be more challenging at home in the first few weeks. ... For most children, this settles within a month as they find their feet. ... Many children hold it together all day at school, then fall apart as soon as they see their ‘safe person’. This isn’t misbehaviour – it’s exhaustion. ... Bring a snack for pick-up time, avoid asking lots of questions straight away, and keep the first 30-60 minutes after school low-demand. Some children regulate best with movement rather than talking, so going to a park, riding a bike or dancing to favourite music can help release the day’s built-up stress. ... For younger children, social stories can help them understand and rehearse situations that feel overwhelming ... Great examples include extra one-on-one time playing a favourite game together, letting your child be the “car DJ” who picks the soundtrack for the drive home ... Spending just 10 minutes a day reading together supports language development, attention, emotional regulation and long-term academic outcomes. ... relating the story to their own experiences all build important skills.
sources.supports: Harder behaviour at home in the first weeks of school is very common and for most children settles within about a month; many children hold it together all day and fall apart with their safe person, which is exhaustion and not misbehaviour; a snack at pick-up, no flood of questions, a low-demand first 30 to 60 minutes; movement instead of talking for some children; one-on-one time as a connection reward; stories that rehearse hard situations and daily shared reading. (Written for the Australian school year; we apply it to the first weeks of first grade in Israel.)

sources.title: Talking about school with kids and teens
sources.publisher: Raising Children Network (Australia); last updated or reviewed 01-07-2024
sources.quote: ‘How was school?’ is a big question. To answer, your child has to sum up a whole day, and that’s often hard to do. ... So it’s easier for them just to say, ‘OK’. ... When your child first gets home from school in the afternoon, they’ll probably be tired and hungry or thinking about other things. ... It’s best to avoid asking your child a lot of questions straight away – this can be overwhelming for your child. You can just let your child know that you’re glad to see them and talk about non-school topics for a while. Younger children will probably also like unpacking their bags and showing you things they’ve brought home before you ask about school. If your child is old enough for homework, saving questions about homework for later can also take the pressure off. ... Simple, positive and specific questions about parts of the day can get your child talking. ... What was fun? ... Who did you hang out with today?
sources.supports: Why 'how was school?' gets 'OK' (summing up a whole day is hard); children come home tired and hungry; do not ask many questions straight away, say you are glad to see them and talk about other things first; younger children like unpacking the bag and showing things; homework questions can wait; simple, positive, specific questions about one part of the day.

sources.title: Primary school: preparing children
sources.publisher: Raising Children Network (Australia); last updated or reviewed 19-07-2024
sources.quote: School is a big transition. Children might need extra emotional support and rest in the first few weeks. ... Read a children’s book about starting school with your child. Reading books about school can help you talk with your child about their feelings. ... Make after-school time a bit special, with a snack and time for you and your child to chat. Be patient if your child tells you every detail about school or clams up completely. You could try saying something like, ‘Tell me one good thing about your day’, rather than asking a lot of questions. ... Your child will probably be very hungry after school. If you give your child a small, healthy snack straight after school, it’ll help to keep them going until dinner. If your child is tired after school, let your child rest and play at home for a few weeks until they’re ready for playdates and after-school activities.
sources.supports: Children may need extra emotional support and rest in the first weeks of school; a snack straight after school because they are very hungry; one small question instead of many; rest and play at home for a few weeks before playdates and after-school activities; reading books about school helps talk about feelings.

sources.publisher: Queensland Health (Queensland Government), tips from developmental paediatrician Dr Angela Owens; published and last updated 30 January 2026
sources.quote: New routines, expectations, teachers and social dynamics can all be exhausting, so it’s very common for behaviour to be more challenging at home in the first few weeks. ... For most children, this settles within a month as they find their feet. ... Many children hold it together all day at school, then fall apart as soon as they see their ‘safe person’. This isn’t misbehaviour – it’s exhaustion. ... Bring a snack for pick-up time, avoid asking lots of questions straight away, and keep the first 30-60 minutes after school low-demand. Some children regulate best with movement rather than talking, so going to a park, riding a bike or dancing to favourite music can help release the day’s built-up stress. ... For younger children, social stories can help them understand and rehearse situations that feel overwhelming ... Great examples include extra one-on-one time playing a favourite game together, letting your child be the “car DJ” who picks the soundtrack for the drive home ... Spending just 10 minutes a day reading together supports language development, attention, emotional regulation and long-term academic outcomes. ... relating the story to their own experiences all build important skills.

sources.title: Talking about school with kids and teens
sources.publisher: Raising Children Network (Australia); last updated or reviewed 01-07-2024
sources.quote: ‘How was school?’ is a big question. To answer, your child has to sum up a whole day, and that’s often hard to do. ... So it’s easier for them just to say, ‘OK’. ... When your child first gets home from school in the afternoon, they’ll probably be tired and hungry or thinking about other things. ... It’s best to avoid asking your child a lot of questions straight away – this can be overwhelming for your child. You can just let your child know that you’re glad to see them and talk about non-school topics for a while. Younger children will probably also like unpacking their bags and showing you things they’ve brought home before you ask about school. If your child is old enough for homework, saving questions about homework for later can also take the pressure off. ... Simple, positive and specific questions about parts of the day can get your child talking. ... What was fun? ... Who did you hang out with today?

sources.title: Primary school: preparing children
sources.publisher: Raising Children Network (Australia); last updated or reviewed 19-07-2024
sources.quote: School is a big transition. Children might need extra emotional support and rest in the first few weeks. ... Read a children’s book about starting school with your child. Reading books about school can help you talk with your child about their feelings. ... Make after-school time a bit special, with a snack and time for you and your child to chat. Be patient if your child tells you every detail about school or clams up completely. You could try saying something like, ‘Tell me one good thing about your day’, rather than asking a lot of questions. ... Your child will probably be very hungry after school. If you give your child a small, healthy snack straight after school, it’ll help to keep them going until dinner. If your child is tired after school, let your child rest and play at home for a few weeks until they’re ready for playdates and after-school activities.

sources.title: Talking about school with kids and teens
sources.publisher: Raising Children Network (Australia); last updated or reviewed 01-07-2024
sources.quote: ‘How was school?’ is a big question. To answer, your child has to sum up a whole day, and that’s often hard to do. ... So it’s easier for them just to say, ‘OK’. ... When your child first gets home from school in the afternoon, they’ll probably be tired and hungry or thinking about other things. ... It’s best to avoid asking your child a lot of questions straight away – this can be overwhelming for your child. You can just let your child know that you’re glad to see them and talk about non-school topics for a while. Younger children will probably also like unpacking their bags and showing you things they’ve brought home before you ask about school. If your child is old enough for homework, saving questions about homework for later can also take the pressure off. ... Simple, positive and specific questions about parts of the day can get your child talking. ... What was fun? ... Who did you hang out with today?
sources.supports: Why 'how was school?' gets 'OK' (summing up a whole day is hard); children come home tired and hungry; do not ask many questions straight away, say you are glad to see them and talk about other things first; younger children like unpacking the bag and showing things; homework questions can wait; simple, positive, specific questions about one part of the day.

sources.title: Primary school: preparing children
sources.publisher: Raising Children Network (Australia); last updated or reviewed 19-07-2024
sources.quote: School is a big transition. Children might need extra emotional support and rest in the first few weeks. ... Read a children’s book about starting school with your child. Reading books about school can help you talk with your child about their feelings. ... Make after-school time a bit special, with a snack and time for you and your child to chat. Be patient if your child tells you every detail about school or clams up completely. You could try saying something like, ‘Tell me one good thing about your day’, rather than asking a lot of questions. ... Your child will probably be very hungry after school. If you give your child a small, healthy snack straight after school, it’ll help to keep them going until dinner. If your child is tired after school, let your child rest and play at home for a few weeks until they’re ready for playdates and after-school activities.
sources.supports: Children may need extra emotional support and rest in the first weeks of school; a snack straight after school because they are very hungry; one small question instead of many; rest and play at home for a few weeks before playdates and after-school activities; reading books about school helps talk about feelings.

sources.title: Back to school: 10 tips from a Developmental Paediatrician
sources.publisher: Queensland Health (Queensland Government), tips from developmental paediatrician Dr Angela Owens; published and last updated 30 January 2026
sources.quote: New routines, expectations, teachers and social dynamics can all be exhausting, so it’s very common for behaviour to be more challenging at home in the first few weeks. ... For most children, this settles within a month as they find their feet. ... Many children hold it together all day at school, then fall apart as soon as they see their ‘safe person’. This isn’t misbehaviour – it’s exhaustion. ... Bring a snack for pick-up time, avoid asking lots of questions straight away, and keep the first 30-60 minutes after school low-demand. Some children regulate best with movement rather than talking, so going to a park, riding a bike or dancing to favourite music can help release the day’s built-up stress. ... For younger children, social stories can help them understand and rehearse situations that feel overwhelming ... Great examples include extra one-on-one time playing a favourite game together, letting your child be the “car DJ” who picks the soundtrack for the drive home ... Spending just 10 minutes a day reading together supports language development, attention, emotional regulation and long-term academic outcomes. ... relating the story to their own experiences all build important skills.
sources.supports: Harder behaviour at home in the first weeks of school is very common and for most children settles within about a month; many children hold it together all day and fall apart with their safe person, which is exhaustion and not misbehaviour; a snack at pick-up, no flood of questions, a low-demand first 30 to 60 minutes; movement instead of talking for some children; one-on-one time as a connection reward; stories that rehearse hard situations and daily shared reading. sources.title: Back to school: 10 tips from a Developmental Paediatrician
sources.publisher: Queensland Health (Queensland Government), tips from developmental paediatrician Dr Angela Owens; published and last updated 30 January 2026
sources.quote: New routines, expectations, teachers and social dynamics can all be exhausting, so it’s very common for behaviour to be more challenging at home in the first few weeks. ... For most children, this settles within a month as they find their feet. ... Many children hold it together all day at school, then fall apart as soon as they see their ‘safe person’. This isn’t misbehaviour – it’s exhaustion. ... Bring a snack for pick-up time, avoid asking lots of questions straight away, and keep the first 30-60 minutes after school low-demand. Some children regulate best with movement rather than talking, so going to a park, riding a bike or dancing to favourite music can help release the day’s built-up stress. ... For younger children, social stories can help them understand and rehearse situations that feel overwhelming ... Great examples include extra one-on-one time playing a favourite game together, letting your child be the “car DJ” who picks the soundtrack for the drive home ... Spending just 10 minutes a day reading together supports language development, attention, emotional regulation and long-term academic outcomes. ... relating the story to their own experiences all build important skills.
sources.supports: Harder behaviour at home in the first weeks of school is very common and for most children settles within about a month; many children hold it together all day and fall apart with their safe person, which is exhaustion and not misbehaviour; a snack at pick-up, no flood of questions, a low-demand first 30 to 60 minutes; movement instead of talking for some children; one-on-one time as a connection reward; stories that rehearse hard situations and daily shared reading. (Written for the Australian school year; we apply it to the first weeks of first grade in Israel.)

sources.title: Primary school: preparing children
sources.publisher: Raising Children Network (Australia); last updated or reviewed 19-07-2024
sources.quote: School is a big transition. Children might need extra emotional support and rest in the first few weeks. ... Read a children’s book about starting school with your child. Reading books about school can help you talk with your child about their feelings. ... Make after-school time a bit special, with a snack and time for you and your child to chat. Be patient if your child tells you every detail about school or clams up completely. You could try saying something like, ‘Tell me one good thing about your day’, rather than asking a lot of questions. ... Your child will probably be very hungry after school. If you give your child a small, healthy snack straight after school, it’ll help to keep them going until dinner. If your child is tired after school, let your child rest and play at home for a few weeks until they’re ready for playdates and after-school activities.
sources.supports: Children may need extra emotional support and rest in the first weeks of school; a snack straight after school because they are very hungry; one small question instead of many; rest and play at home for a few weeks before playdates and after-school activities; reading books about school helps talk about feelings.
